sections.summary: Putnam contrasts progress in syntax with the confused treatment of word meaning, then examines extension, intension, and their idealizations. Two traditional assumptions—that knowing meaning is an individual psychological state and that meaning determines extension—are identified as jointly untenable.

Combining this restriction with traditional semantics implies that identical psychological states fix identical extensions, the consequence the essay will challenge.

Artifact names and many other parts of speech can behave similarly, while some derivative and grammatical words retain a more purely criterial character.

sections.summary: Putnam reviews Quine’s criticisms of analyticity, centrality, synonymy, and unrevisability, including the pressure from scientific theory change. Obligatory stereotype knowledge can remain part of meaning without guaranteeing truth or analyticity, avoiding those particular objections.

sections.summary: Stereotypes, expert-guided extensions, and elicited explanations constrain translation without independently determining it. Putnam argues for a wider evidence base than assent and dissent, while acknowledging the need for cultural and belief-related constraints.

sections.summary: Davidsonian truth-theoretic semantics faces a tension between extensional correctness, informative translation, and avoiding the word being explained. Putnam also rejects restricting linguistic evidence to whole-sentence dispositions when constituent-level elicitation and native competence are available.

sections.summary: Carnap-style intensions leave their psychological grasp unexplained and omit social cooperation and indexical reference. Vagueness does not repair these defects, though enriched formal models that include speakers and contexts may remain useful.

sections.summary: Semantic markers identify highly central category features such as animal or artifact without making them absolutely unrevisable. Putnam preserves the distinction between markers and other stereotype features while rejecting their use as necessary-and-sufficient definitions.

sections.summary: The proposed meaning vector includes syntactic markers, semantic markers, stereotype, and extension, with the last component not attributed to individual knowledge. Twin Earth and bilingual synonymy illustrate its consequences, and the conclusion calls for semantics that includes society and the external world.

sections.summary: Dijkstra argues that programs should make the relationship between static text and dynamic execution easy to understand. Structured sequencing, conditionals, procedures, and loops provide independent coordinates for reasoning about progress and variable values, whereas unrestricted jumps obscure them; mechanically eliminating jumps alone does not restore clarity.

oracle.title: Science and Statistics
oracle.abstract: Aspects of scientific method are discussed: In particular, its representation as a motivated iteration in which, in succession, practice confronts theory, and theory, practice. Rapid progress requires sufficient flexibility to profit from such confrontations, and the ability to devise parsimonious but effective models, to worry selectively about model inadequacies and to employ mathematics skillfully but appropriately. The development of statistical methods at Rothamsted Experimental Station by Sir Ronald Fisher is used to illustrate these themes.

sections.title: Science as iterative model criticism

sections.summary: Scientific learning alternates between theory and practice through feedback from model failures. Flexibility, parsimony, selective concern for consequential errors, and appropriately applied mathematics make this iteration effective.

sections.summary: Fisher’s Rothamsted work illustrates how close engagement with real observations generates theory, from tea tasting and bacterial counts to extreme values and crop-yield trends. Orthogonal polynomials and residual checks show the interaction between fitting, criticism, and substantive explanations.

sections.summary: Rainfall–yield modeling illustrates parsimonious distributed lags, while potato trials motivate ANOVA, interactions, split-plot correction, and randomization. A simulation shows that error dependence can invalidate both parametric and rank tests unless randomization restores the needed protection.

sections.summary: Standard regression significance tests rely on an error structure that fails when unrelated dependent and explanatory series are highly autocorrelated. Sampling variability in correlations can therefore produce high fit without a genuine relationship.

sections.summary: Simulations of independent random walks and integrated moving-average series produce frequent false significance and high fit, increasingly so with more irrelevant regressors. Differencing sharply improves results, though residual moving-average dependence can still distort tests.
